payload.throughline: Separate the comparison axes first, then relate mobility, resources, participation, care, and outcomes without turning a pattern into an unsupported cause.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes starting check: separate who is compared from whether social rank changes. This check neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.

Mobility uses two independent axes. Intergenerational compares people across generations; intragenerational follows one person over time. Vertical changes social rank; horizontal changes position at a similar rank.
Ask the time question first: parent and child, or one person at two times? Then ask the rank question: higher or lower standing, or roughly similar standing?

Meritocracy is a claim that ability and effort determine rewards. A case may invoke that claim even when it also reports unequal opportunities; invocation is not proof that the system is actually meritocratic.
Use a two-axis matrix: rows are across generations versus within one life; columns are changed rank versus similar rank. Evaluate meritocracy in a separate claim box.

A nurse whose parent was a factory worker is an across-generation comparison; if the nurse position has higher rank, it is intergenerational vertical mobility. If the account says effort alone produced the outcome, it invokes meritocracy, but I still inspect barriers before accepting that premise.
A teacher moves to a curriculum role with similar pay and standing during the same career. One person changes position within a life, and rank stays similar: intragenerational horizontal mobility.
A manager’s child becomes a manager in another industry. The comparison is across generations, but rank is similar: intergenerational horizontal mobility.
With support, mark the time axis, mark the rank axis, and then identify any separate meritocracy statement.
With less support, use the cues across generations/within life and changed rank/similar rank.
Classify a fresh mobility case without an answer-bearing cue.
Boundary: changing employers is not automatically vertical mobility. Rank must change. A story praising effort may invoke meritocracy, but praise alone does not establish equal opportunity.
Near-use exit: classify a fresh trajectory on both mobility axes.
Changed-task exit: identify and evaluate a meritocracy invocation in a mobility account.
Repair the classification function: write one answer for time and a separate answer for rank before combining them.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new person, generation comparison, occupation, and rank pattern.
Repair the claim-evaluation function: underline ability-or-effort language, then separate the claim from evidence about opportunity and constraints.
Fresh re-entry: evaluate a new mobility account that combines effort language with a different structural barrier.
Recap: inter/intra answers when; vertical/horizontal answers rank change. Meritocracy language explains rewards through ability and effort but does not prove equal opportunity.
Low-stakes starting check: decide whether a case turns on unmet basic needs, a society-relative shortfall, or blocked participation. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.

Absolute poverty concerns inability to secure basic necessities. Relative poverty compares resources with prevailing standards in a society. Social exclusion concerns blocked participation and access, often through segregation or isolation.

Use the basic-needs check first. If basic necessities cannot be secured, absolute poverty is supported. If necessities are secured but resources prevent participation in ordinary social life, relative poverty is supported.
For social exclusion, trace a mechanism: separation or isolation reduces contact with schools, jobs, transport, services, or networks, which restricts participation.
Keep three boxes: survival floor, social comparison, and participation pathway. Poverty labels describe resource conditions; exclusion describes a process that blocks connection and access.

A household unable to obtain food and shelter fits absolute poverty. A household meeting those needs but unable to participate in ordinary local activities because its resources are far below the social norm fits relative poverty. A segregated neighborhood cut off from transport shows an exclusion pathway.
Case A lacks reliable food and shelter: basic necessities fail, so absolute poverty fits.
Case B has food and shelter but cannot afford routine digital access used for school and work in that society: the decisive comparison is relative.
Case C is physically separated from jobs and clinics by transit isolation: segregation and isolation restrict participation, supporting social exclusion.
With support, mark basic needs, social comparison, and any segregation-to-access pathway.
With less support, use the cue trio survival floor, social norm, or blocked participation.
Classify a fresh poverty or exclusion case without an answer-bearing hint.

Boundary: social exclusion can occur without absolute poverty, and poverty does not by itself prove exclusion. Detailed poverty-threshold calculations and welfare policy evaluation are outside this KC.
Near-use exit: distinguish absolute from relative poverty in a fresh resource case.
Changed-task exit: trace segregation or isolation to restricted access and participation.
Repair the poverty contrast: check basic necessities before comparing the household with prevailing social standards.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new household with different necessities and society-relative participation cues.
Repair the exclusion function: name the separating condition, the blocked connection, and the participation consequence.
Fresh re-entry: trace a new isolation mechanism to a different resource and participation limit.
Recap: absolute asks whether basic needs are met; relative asks how resources compare with social norms; exclusion traces segregation or isolation to blocked access and participation.
Low-stakes starting check: identify whether the measured difference is a health outcome, a care-system process, both, or neither. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.

Health disparities are group-patterned differences in health status or outcomes. Health-care disparities are group-patterned differences in access to or delivery of care. Class, gender, and race can pattern either domain.

Sort the measure, not the topic. Mortality, disease prevalence, and life expectancy are outcomes. Insurance coverage, appointment availability, wait time, utilization, and treatment delivery are health-care measures.
A case can contain both types. Describe observed class, gender, or race patterning, but do not claim that one observed difference caused the other unless the evidence supports that inference.
Use two columns: health outcome and health-care process. Put each measure in one column before relating them. A shared group label does not turn correlation into causation.

If one racial group has a higher disease rate, I classify a health disparity. If that group also has longer appointment waits, I classify a health-care disparity too. The table alone supports patterning, not a causal claim that wait time produced the disease difference.
A graph shows lower average life expectancy by income group: the measure is an outcome, so it is a class-patterned health disparity.
A table shows fewer offered follow-up appointments by gender group: the measure is access or delivery, so it is a gender-patterned health-care disparity.
With support, label each measure outcome or care process, then name the group pattern without adding causality.
With less support, use the cue pair health status versus access or delivery.
Classify a fresh disparity measure without an answer-bearing cue.

Boundary: a hospital quality-management detail is not automatically a disparity; a group-patterned access or delivery difference must be shown. Two co-occurring disparities do not by themselves establish causation.
Near-use exit: classify a fresh group-patterned health outcome.
Changed-task exit: separate simultaneous care-system and outcome differences in one case.
Repair the classification function: name the exact measure and ask whether it records health status or a care-system process.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new outcome measure and a new population pattern.
Repair the paired-measure function: place each measure in its own column and state only the observed relation.
Fresh re-entry: separate new access and outcome measures without inferring an unsupported cause.

Recap: outcomes belong to health disparities; access and delivery belong to health-care disparities. Patterning by class, gender, or race can occur in either, and observed association is not causal proof.

question_evidence_plan.changed_dimension_detail: Changes from classifying a trajectory to evaluating an effort-based meritocracy claim against stated opportunity constraints.
Uses promotion-program access rather than training access while preserving claim-versus-evidence evaluation.
Changes from classifying a household resource condition to tracing segregation and network isolation into restricted employment participation.
Uses language isolation and public-information access rather than spatial segregation and employment access while preserving the exclusion pathway.
Changes from classifying one outcome measure to sorting simultaneous access and outcome measures while withholding causal inference.
Uses screening availability and diagnosis timing instead of appointment availability and hospitalization while preserving paired sorting and the causal nonclaim.
